interviewQuestions.question: Why do two-tower models scale to hundreds of millions of items?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start with the architecture: a two-tower model has two separate networks — one embeds the user (plus context), one embeds the item — and never combines their features until a final dot product. That separation is the whole trick.

Because the item tower doesn't depend on the user at all, you can run it once, offline, over your *entire* catalog and store every item's embedding in an index ahead of time. At request time you only need to run the user tower once, then do an approximate nearest-neighbor search (FAISS, ScaNN) against that precomputed item index — which is sublinear in catalog size, not a forward pass per candidate item.

Concretely, this is why YouTube and Instagram use two-tower models for candidate generation specifically: it lets them cut hundreds of millions of items down to a few hundred candidates in milliseconds, before handing off to a heavier, feature-rich ranking model that can afford to actually run a full network per candidate on that much smaller shortlist.

**Testing:** whether you understand the precompute-vs-serve-time trade that makes retrieval at scale possible — this is the same principle behind every large-scale embedding-based search system, not just recommenders.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why two-tower models scale

interviewQuestions.question: Why can't a neural collaborative filtering (NCF) model be used for candidate generation over a huge catalog the way a two-tower model can, even though NCF is more expressive?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The blocker is architectural, not a matter of NCF being less powerful — it's actually more expressive, which is exactly what makes it unsuitable for this specific job. NCF combines the user and item embeddings early, concatenating or otherwise merging them *before* feeding the joint representation through an MLP to produce a score. That early combination is what lets it learn genuinely non-linear interactions a dot product can't — an AND-like condition such as "this user loves this item only when it's both recent and in their favorite genre" — but it also means the score for a specific user-item pair cannot be computed without both pieces present at the same time. There's no way to precompute an item's "score contribution" independent of which user is asking, because the model's whole point is that user and item features interact non-linearly together, not through two separable pieces that combine via a simple operation.

This forces NCF into an unavoidable per-candidate forward pass: to score a user against a candidate catalog of a million items, you have to run the MLP a million times, once per candidate, because each one needs the actual combined user+item input. A two-tower model's separate towers only combine via a plain dot product at the very end, which is exactly why item embeddings can be computed once, offline, independent of any user — the item tower never needs to know which user it'll eventually be compared against, so its output can be cached in an index ahead of time and searched with approximate nearest neighbors rather than recomputed per request.

The practical implication: NCF's expressiveness is genuinely valuable, but specifically for the *ranking* stage, where the candidate set has already been narrowed to a few hundred items and a forward pass per candidate is affordable — not for candidate generation over the full catalog, which is exactly why production systems typically use two-tower models for retrieval and a richer model like NCF for the ranking stage that follows.

**Testing:** whether you can connect the early-combination architecture directly to the precomputation constraint it breaks, not just state that NCF is "more expensive."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why NCF can't do candidate generation like two-tower models can

interviewQuestions.question: A team claims their new deep-learning-based recommender has finally solved cold start because it's more powerful than their old matrix factorization system. What would you push back on?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd push back on the premise directly: model depth and expressiveness address a completely different problem than cold start does, and no amount of additional network capacity changes that. Cold start's core issue is a total absence of interaction data for a specific user or item — there's simply nothing for any model, however sophisticated, to learn a meaningful ID-based embedding from, because an ID embedding is learned entirely from observed interactions, and a new user or item has none. A deeper network with more parameters doesn't create data that doesn't exist; it can only extract more signal from data that's actually there. If the only inputs are learned ID embeddings, a brand-new ID's embedding is just as untrained and uninformative in a deep neural model as it would be in plain matrix factorization — the depth of the network is irrelevant to a problem that's fundamentally about missing input, not insufficient model capacity.

What I'd ask the team to check: does their model actually incorporate content features — item text or image embeddings, user demographics or onboarding signals — alongside the ID embeddings, or is it purely ID-based collaborative signal wrapped in a deeper architecture? If it's the latter, whatever apparent cold-start improvement they're observing is likely either noise, a change in some other part of the pipeline, or an artifact of how they're measuring it — not a genuine fix. If they have added content features, then the actual credit belongs to that hybrid design decision (falling back to content signal when the ID embedding is untrained), not to "deep learning" as a general claim — and I'd want that distinction made explicit in how the team communicates the result, since conflating the two leads to false confidence that scaling the model further would keep improving cold-start performance on its own.

**Testing:** whether you separate model capacity from data availability as genuinely distinct axes, and can identify the specific architectural change (content features) that would actually justify the team's claim.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Challenging a claim that deep learning 'solves' cold start
